docs.title: Welcome to Badgers
docs.text:
Badgers is a python library for generating bad data - more precisely: to augment existing data with data quality deficits such as outliers, missing values, noise, etc.

As a basic principle, badgers provides a set of objects (called generators) that follow a simple API: each generator provides a generator(X,y,**params) function that takes as argument X (the input features), y (the class labels, the regression target, or None), a set of specific parameters and returns the transformed Xt and yt.

Why would you generate bad data? you might ask (and you should! isn't that honestly a strange idea?).

We think data quality has to be taken seriously. With badgers we hope to provide a tool that can help manage and understand the impact of data quality in a systematic and controlled way.

You might think of using badgers for things like robustness analysis (i.e., how does my model or my data analysis pipeline performs in the presence of noise, outliers, missing values, data drift, etc.), or for chaos data engineering (e.g., what happens if we inject quality defects into production systems?).

Badgers provides a set of predefined generators for different modalities (tabular data, time series, text, etc.) and different data quality problems (outliers, noise, drift, etc.). Of course many data quality problems are use case dependent and it is not possible to implement all generators. Therefore, the idea is that badgers can serve as a structure for developing novel generators (see how to develop novel generators in the dev-tutorials section).

Want to try badgers? Then go to the getting started section or dive into the tutorials section.

A big thanks to Daniel Seifert for taking the time to investigate and automate all the many things that make our lives as package contributors easier.

docs.title: Core Module
docs.text: The core module serves as the foundation of the Badgers framework, providing essential building blocks and infrastructure that other components rely on.

docs.title: Main Responsibilities:
docs.text:
1. Base Classes: Defines the fundamental GeneratorMixin abstract base class that all generators must inherit from, ensuring a consistent interface across the entire system.

  2. Standardized Interface: Enforces a uniform generate(X, y, **params) method signature that returns transformed data (Xt, yt) for all generators.

  3. Input Preprocessing: Provides decorator functions (preprocess_inputs) that automatically validate and convert input data to standardized formats (numpy arrays).

  4. Pipeline Infrastructure: Implements the Pipeline class that enables chaining multiple generators together in sequential workflows.

  5. Utility Functions: Offers helper functions for common operations like probability normalization and random number generation.

docs.title: Generators Module
docs.text: The generators module contains the actual implementation of various data transformation algorithms, organized by data type categories.

docs.title: Main Responsibilities:
docs.text:
1. Data Transformation Implementation: Houses concrete implementations of various data generation techniques across different data domains:
  2. Tabular data transformations (outliers, drift, imbalance, missingness, noise)
  3. Time series modifications (changepoints, seasons, trends, transmission errors)
  4. Graph-based manipulations

  5. Text transformation tools

  6. Domain-Specific Organization: Structures generators by data type categories, making it easy to find and use appropriate transformations for specific data modalities.

  7. Extensibility: Provides a plug-and-play architecture where new generators can be easily added by following the established GeneratorMixin interface.

docs.title: Benchmarks Module
docs.text: The benchmarks package provides a systematic framework for measuring performance (time/memory) of all generators. It lives outside the main badgers source to avoid coupling.

docs.title: Architecture (3 Layers)
docs.text:
1. Registration Layer (models.py, registry.py, scenarios/, generators/):
  2. Scenario dataclasses define reusable data factories for each data type (tabular, time series, graph, text).
  3. GeneratorBenchmark ties a generator class to its scenarios.

  4. The Registry auto-discovers _*.py registration modules from benchmarks/generators/.

  5. Execution Layer (runner.py, cli.py):

  6. run_performance() measures wall-clock time and peak memory over multiple iterations.

  7. CLI provides run, baseline, and compare subcommands.

  8. Analysis Layer (comparator.py):

  9. compare_results() diffs two result sets and flags regressions (>20% time, >30% memory).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
# Run all benchmarks (performance)
python -m benchmarks run

# Filter by generator category
python -m benchmarks run --generators tabular_data.outliers

# Save a baseline for regression detection
python -m benchmarks baseline save --name v1.0

# Compare latest results against a baseline
python -m benchmarks compare --baseline v1.0

docs.title: Adding a New Generator to Benchmarks
docs.text:
Create a _<name>.py file in the appropriate benchmarks/generators/<category>/ directory:

from benchmarks.models import GeneratorBenchmark
from benchmarks.registry import register
from benchmarks.scenarios.tabular import SCENARIO_SMALL_BLOBS, SCENARIO_MEDIUM_BLOBS
from badgers.generators.tabular_data.noise import AdditiveNoiseGenerator

register(GeneratorBenchmark(
    generator_cls=AdditiveNoiseGenerator,
    name="AdditiveNoise",
    module_path="tabular_data.noise",
    default_params={"distribution": scipy.stats.norm(scale=0.5)},
    scenarios=[SCENARIO_SMALL_BLOBS, SCENARIO_MEDIUM_BLOBS],
))

The registry auto-discovers all _*.py files — no other changes needed.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Tests live under tests/ and use pytest with function-based tests (no unittest.TestCase classes). The test structure mirrors the source layout:

tests/
├── conftest.py                  # shared fixtures (e.g., rng)
├── core/                        # tests for badgers.core
├── benchmarks/                  # tests for the benchmarks package
└── generators/
    ├── tabular_data/
    │   ├── conftest.py          # tabular-specific fixtures
    │   ├── test_outliers.py
    │   ├── test_noise.py
    │   └── ...
    ├── time_series/
    │   ├── conftest.py          # time-series fixtures (sine, random walk)
    │   └── ...
    ├── graph/
    │   ├── conftest.py          # graph fixtures (Erdős-Rényi)
    │   └── ...
    └── text/
        ├── conftest.py          # text fixtures (word list)
        └── ...

docs.title: Key Conventions
docs.text:
• Fixtures over classes: Each data type has a conftest.py with reusable fixtures (e.g., tabular_small, time_series_sine, graph_erdos_renyi, text_word_list). Fixtures return (X, y) tuples with deterministic random seeds.
  • Flat test functions: Tests are plain test_<subject>__<behavior> functions (double underscore separator), not methods on TestCase classes.
  • Generator tests are independent: Generator correctness is tested directly via pytest, not through the benchmark framework's functional checks. This keeps tests fast, focused, and free of benchmark infrastructure coupling.

docs.title: Running Tests
docs.text:
# Run all tests
pytest tests/

# Run only generator tests
pytest tests/generators/

# Run a specific category
pytest tests/generators/tabular_data/ -v

docs.title: Architectural Decisions
docs.text: This section records significant architectural decisions made during the project's evolution. Each decision includes the rationale and date of adoption.

docs.title: ADR-1: Strict Separation of Tests and Benchmarks (2026-06-23)
docs.text:
Decision: Unit tests (tests/) and performance benchmarks (benchmarks/) serve distinct purposes and must not overlap.

Concern Unit Tests Benchmarks Purpose Catch logic bugs Measure perf, detect regressions Data Small, varied (numpy/pandas × 1D/2D) Medium-large, standardized Data source Per-type conftest.py fixtures benchmarks/scenarios/ Speed Fast (<1ms each) Measured (timed iterations) Checks Exact assertions Performance stats only

Rationale: The benchmarks module originally duplicated functional assertions via FunctionalCheck/FunctionalResult. These were removed so that tests/ is the single source of truth for correctness and benchmarks focus exclusively on timing, memory, and regression detection. Generator correctness is tested directly via pytest, not through the benchmark framework.

docs.title: ADR-2: Per-Data-Type Pytest Fixture Architecture (2026-06-23)
docs.text:
Decision: Tests use per-data-type conftest.py files with parametrized pytest fixtures instead of unittest.TestCase classes or a monolithic fixture file.

tests/
  conftest.py                          # shared: rng fixture only
  generators/
    tabular_data/
      conftest.py                      # tabular_data, tabular_data_labeled fixtures
    time_series/
      conftest.py                      # time_series_sine, time_series_walk fixtures
    graph/
      conftest.py                      # graph_erdos_renyi fixture
    text/
      conftest.py                      # text_word_list fixture

Naming conventions: - Fixtures: prefixed with data type (tabular_data, time_series_sine, graph_erdos_renyi, text_word_list) - Test functions: test_<subject>__<behavior> with double underscore separator (e.g., test_gaussian_noise__increases_variance) - No unittest.TestCase classes — flat pytest functions only - Only numpy and pandas input types (no list_1D/list_2D)

Rationale: Fixtures are auto-discovered by pytest's conftest.py mechanism, scoped to the nearest directory. This keeps test data close to the tests that use it, avoids a single monolithic fixture file, and enables pytest's built-in parametrization for testing across input types.

docs.title: ADR-3: Benchmark Registration via Auto-Discovered Modules (2026-06-24)
docs.text:
Decision: Each generator category has a _*.py registration module in benchmarks/generators/<data_type>/ that imports generator classes and calls register(GeneratorBenchmark(...)). The registry auto-discovers these modules.

Key constraint: Density-based generators (e.g., HistogramSamplingGenerator) must only use SCENARIO_SMALL_BLOBS (2D) because they raise on >5D input.

Rationale: Decouples benchmark definitions from the benchmark runner. Adding a new generator to benchmarks is a single register() call in the appropriate _*.py file — no other changes needed.

docs.title: ADR-4: Vectorized NumPy Over Python Loops (2026-06-26)
docs.text:
Decision: All generator implementations must prefer batched/vectorized NumPy operations over Python-level for loops, especially when n_samples can be large.

Three canonical patterns:

  1. Per-row RNG → batched RNG: Replace [rng.exponential(size=d) for _ in range(n)] with rng.exponential(size=(n, d))
  2. Per-column .iloc/.choice → integer array indexing: Replace np.stack([rng.choice(X.iloc[:, i], ...) for i in range(d)]) with X.values[row_idx, np.arange(d)]
  3. Batch variants for utilities: When a utility operates on a single sample (e.g., random_spherical_coordinate), also provide a batch version (random_spherical_coordinates) accepting arrays with axis= parameters

When NOT to vectorize: small n_samples (≤10), algorithms requiring sequential state (e.g., rejection sampling with unknown iteration count).

Rationale: Badgers generators often produce many samples at once. Python loops over RNG calls or pandas .iloc accesses are orders of magnitude slower than batched NumPy operations. The O(d²) np.prod(sin_phis[:i]) pattern in random_spherical_coordinate was also fixed to O(d) via np.cumprod.

docs.title: ADR-5: Baseline-Based Regression Detection (2026-06-24)
docs.text:
Decision: Benchmarks support a baseline workflow for detecting performance regressions with defined thresholds:

python -m benchmarks run --iterations 10
python -m benchmarks baseline save --name v0.0.13
python -m benchmarks compare --baseline v0.0.13

Regression thresholds: >20% time increase or >30% memory increase triggers a flag in comparator.py.

Rationale: Baselines are versioned snapshots of generator performance. They enable automated detection of performance regressions before merging, providing a quantitative gate for optimization work.

docs.title: Causal defect family: three-layer design
docs.text:
1. Structure (static, user-provided): the structural nx.DiGraph (latent variables), the column_mapping (node -> integer column), and an optional observation nx.DiGraph (measurement nodes, R_<name> indicator nodes, derivation edges). Validation is functions in badgers.core.causal_graph.
  2. Fitted knowledge (the DGP protocol): backends implement exactly one operation — fit_node(node, parents, data) — and expose two views: response(node, parent_values) (the fitted deterministic part) and draw_noise(node, rng, n) (the node's own shock; parametric or empirical). fit(X) is a provided topological loop. The DGP is immutable and rngless: every stochastic method takes the caller's rng; nothing retains training data.
  3. Deficit algebra (written once, backend-blind): the generic DGPMixin cascade — intervene(rows, nodes, values=None, *, rng=None) (Pearl surgery on given rows: fix the nodes, recompute ALL descendants in topological order with fresh noise; intervened nodes stay pinned) and sample(rng, n) — both start by calling the pick_parameters(rng) hook (default: self; the PyMC backend overrides it to pin one coherent posterior draw per cascade). Structure edits are free functions in badgers.core.dgp.edits (the DGP itself has NO edit methods): scale_edge/remove_edge (edge reweighting with variance-budget calibration — no coefficient access needed), exogenize (make a node a root; INTERVENTION-ONLY semantics), set_form (replace a node's functional form), add_edge_contribution (ANM-scoped cheap edge addition). Re- estimation after a structural modification is out of scope: build the modified SCM with the wrapped library's own API, fit it, and wrap it again with GcmSCMDGP/PyMCSCMDGP. Edits return read-only views and never mutate the base DGP. Indicator derivation from the observation graph lives in the missingness generator (structure-layer helpers + generator-local firing/spread logic).

Backend selection is object injection only (dgp=... / use_dgp). Deficit semantics live in the generators; they never see which backend ran. The generator carries NO structure of its own: CausalGenerator.__init__ accepts only random_generator= and dgp=, derives its graph/column_mapping views from the DGP, and there is no generator-side fit or implicit default backend — a missing dgp= is a hard error. Unfitted DGPs are fitted lazily on first generate(X).

docs.title: Benchmarking
docs.text: Badgers includes a benchmarking framework to measure performance (time/memory) of all generators. It helps detect regressions when refactoring or optimizing code.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
# Run all benchmarks (performance)
python -m benchmarks run

# Filter by module path
python -m benchmarks run --generators tabular_data.outliers

docs.title: run — Execute Benchmarks
docs.text:
python -m benchmarks run [--generators FILTER] [--iterations N] [--timeout S]
Option Default Description --generators (all) Filter by module path prefix, e.g. tabular_data.outliers --iterations 5 Number of iterations for performance measurement --timeout 60 Timeout in seconds per scenario

Results are saved as JSON to .benchmarks/results/run_<branch>_<timestamp>.json. This directory is gitignored — results are local-only.

docs.title: baseline — Manage Baselines
docs.text:
python -m benchmarks baseline save [--name NAME]
python -m benchmarks baseline list

Baselines are snapshots of results used for regression detection. Save a baseline after verifying all checks pass on a known-good commit.

Baselines are stored in .benchmarks/baselines/ (gitignored, local-only).

docs.title: compare — Detect Regressions
docs.text:
python -m benchmarks compare [--baseline NAME] [--target PATH]

Compares the latest (or specified) results against a baseline and reports regressions:

  • Time regression: >20% increase in mean execution time
  • Memory regression: >30% increase in peak memory usage

docs.title: Performance Metrics
docs.text:
• Wall-clock time: min, max, mean, median, stddev over N iterations
  • Peak memory: measured via tracemalloc

    generator_cls=AdditiveNoiseGenerator,

    default_params={"distribution": scipy.stats.norm(scale=0.5)},
    scenarios=[SCENARIO_SMALL_BLOBS, SCENARIO_MEDIUM_BLOBS],

The registry auto-discovers all _*.py files — no other registration needed.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
• Causal generators: labels are internal generator state (breaking). The causal defect generators (CausalDriftGenerator, CausalMissingnessGenerator, CausalImbalanceGenerator, CausalNoiseGenerator, CausalAdditiveNoiseGenerator) no longer return deficit labels in yt: generate() returns (Xt, None) and each generator exposes its own boolean label getter aligned with the rows of the last generated output — (get_drift_labels(), get_missing_labels(), get_imbalance_labels(), get_noise_labels() (both noise generators), get_outliers_labels(). Calling a getter before generate() raises RuntimeError. The base class owns the storage slot (deficit_labels_); each generator owns its getter.

  • CausalGenerator._validate replaced by two raise-only helpers. _validate(X, perturbation_nodes) (which mixed validation with graph-derivative computation and returned a 5-tuple) is split into _validate_structure(X) (graph/DAG, column count, column_mapping coverage and indices) and _validate_perturbation_nodes(nodes) (non-empty list of known nodes). Neither returns anything — the mapping is self.column_mapping. The dead order member and the graph algebra (descendants/exogenous/perturb_cols) moved into the only generator that used them (CausalOutlierPropagationGenerator).

  • PyMCDGP and the old badgers.core.dgp module are removed. The causal defect generators now fit a per-node data generation process behind the new DGP protocol (badgers.core.dgp is a package). Backends are injected as objects (dgp=... / use_dgp); PyMC-specific parameters (n_samples_mcmc, fit_dgp) no longer appear in fit(...).

  • CausalGenerator.fit removed AND the graph=/column_mapping= generator-side structure is gone (breaking). The DGP is the ONLY structure a causal generator accepts: the constructor is CausalGenerator(random_generator=..., dgp=None) and the only structure param anywhere on the generator is dgp= (or use_dgp(dgp)). The DGP carries graph and column_mapping itself — build one with e.g. dgp = GcmSCMDGP(scm).fit(X) (see docs/dev/Using-DGPs.ipynb). Unfitted DGPs are fitted lazily on first generate(X) (DGP.is_fitted is respected).
  • fit signature change for the causal defect family: fit(X, graph, column_mapping, dgp=None) — n_samples_mcmc and fit_dgp are gone.
  • AdditiveNoiseGenerator (new, non-causal): injects noise drawn from any frozen scipy distribution object (distribution=....rvs(size, random_state=rng)) instead of hard-coded Gaussian white noise (e.g.scipy.stats.laplace(scale=1),scipy.stats.t(df=3)).noise_stdis a global magnitude multiplier (1.0 = raw draw); what you pass is what is added — no rescaling. Optionalperturbation_nodes` restricts the noise to a column subset.
  • CausalAdditiveNoiseGenerator (new, causal): same swappable distribution at the perturbation nodes, with descendant recomputation via the DGP (dgp.intervene — Pearl surgery). Row gating is delegated to a selector (default: every row fires); strictly in-place (no n_copies).
  • GaussianNoiseGenerator removed (breaking). It is a strict special case of the new AdditiveNoiseGenerator: replace GaussianNoiseGenerator().generate(X, y, noise_std=0.5) with AdditiveNoiseGenerator().generate(X, y, distribution=scipy.stats.norm(scale=0.5)). (Note the semantic shift: the old class standardized first, so its noise_std was column-relative; the new API adds the frozen distribution's raw draws — pass the per-column scale yourself.) GaussianNoiseClassesGenerator (per-class noise) remains; the time-series Local/GlobalGaussianNoiseGenerator are unrelated and unchanged.
  • CausalEdgePerturbationGenerator is removed for this release (deferred to future work). The relationship-level (edge weight) defect — scaling one edge coefficient and recomputing the child marginal-preserving — was developed behind the family API but is not part of the 0.0.15 surface: the generator, its tests and the "Perturbing Edge Strength" tutorial are removed. The underlying edits.scale_edge DGP edit remains in badgers.core.dgp.edits (and is tested), so re-introducing the generator is a small follow-up.
  • CausalImbalanceGenerator no longer requires a DGP (breaking): the generator is a pure row-subset (quantile-range truncation); the kept rows' parents are unchanged, so no structural equation is re-evaluated. The dead mechanism/mechanism_cause/mechanism_rate parameters, the on-demand OLS fit, and the no-op propagate pass are removed — the signature is now generate(X, y, perturbation_nodes=None, quantile_range=(0.5, 1.0)). This is the first generator in the causal family whose generate needs neither a DGP nor any random numbers (selection-side only).
  • CausalMissingnessGenerator is chooser-only (breaking): missingness is an observation-layer defect — it only hides cells (writes NaN) and does NOT cascade to descendants. The missingness_rule mechanism parameter, the on-demand DGP fit, and the any/all NaN-propagation passes are removed; the fire mask comes from a selector object (see the selector bullet below). Signature: generate(X, y, perturbation_nodes=None, selector=None).
  • String mechanism flags replaced by selector objects (breaking). The row-gating parameters of the causal defect generators (CausalDriftGenerator, CausalMissingnessGenerator, CausalNoiseGenerator, CausalAdditiveNoiseGenerator) are now a single selector= parameter holding a callable from badgers.core.selectors; None defaults to "every row fires" (AlwaysSelector semantics). The mechanism/mechanism_cause/ mechanism_rate strings and the _fire_masks string dispatcher are removed. Migration:
  • mechanism="always" → omit selector (or AlwaysSelector(nodes)).
  • mechanism="random", mechanism_rate=r → selector=BernoulliSelector(nodes, rate=r, rng=gen.random_generator).
  • mechanism="self", mechanism_rate=r → selector=TopQuantileSelector(nodes, column_mapping, quantile=1-r).
  • mechanism="observed", mechanism_cause=c, mechanism_rate=r → selector=TopQuantileSelector(nodes, column_mapping, quantile=1-r, drivers=c). Intensity lives on the selector object: rate and quantile are now CONSTRUCTOR arguments of BernoulliSelector/ExactCountSelector/ TopQuantileSelector (previously rate was a __call__ kwarg and quantile a call kwarg) — so an intensity sweep means constructing a new selector. AlwaysSelector was added (the all-rows preset).
  • RandomSamplingClassesGenerator takes a selector (breaking). The proportion_classes call kwarg is removed; pass instead selector=ClassSelector("cls", column_mapping, proportions, rng=...) from badgers.core.selectors, where proportions maps each class column to {class_value: proportion}. Class columns are columns of X (the target y is being deprecated as a data carrier: selection no longer reads it). The selector's fire mask is the standard contract (True = deficit); the generator's deficit is DROPPING the fired rows (subsampling), so the output is smaller than the input. Classes absent from the mapping are kept as-is; proportions are shares of the total row count, clipped to the rows available in each class. The class variable must be a column of X resolved via column_mapping (the target y is deprecated as a data carrier and is never read for selection). selector=None is a no-op. Migration: generate(X, y, proportion_classes={0: 0.5, ...}) → generate(np.column_stack([X, y]), y, selector=ClassSelector("cls", {"cls": n_features}, {"cls": {0: 0.5, ...}}, rng=rng)). Note the new semantics sample WITHOUT replacement (the old implementation duplicated rows when a proportion exceeded the class size).
  • Outlier labels are internal generator state, no longer returned in yt (breaking). All outlier generators (HyperCubeSampling, ZScoreSamplingGenerator, HypersphereSamplingGenerator, UniformInstanceAttributeSampling, IndependentHistogramsGenerator, HistogramSamplingGenerator, LowDensitySamplingGenerator, CausalOutlierPropagationGenerator, and StructuredOutlierGenerator) now expose get_outliers_labels(): a boolean vector aligned with the rows of the LAST generated output, True where the row is an outlier, False where it is an original row. generate() returns (Xt, y) with y a pure pass-through (and y=None signatures throughout — the previous "original"/"outliers" string arrays are gone). Calling get_outliers_labels() before generate() raises RuntimeError. Migration: Xt, yt = gen.generate(X) followed by yt == "outliers" → Xt, y = gen.generate(X) followed by gen.get_outliers_labels().
  • Selector scores may now be fractional (additive contract extension). A selector's per-row value may be a float in [0, 1] — the PROBABILITY that the deficit is applied — where boolean masks remain the degenerate (deterministic) case. A selector never draws randomness for these rates; realization belongs to the consuming generator (a gating consumer fires Bernoulli-wise, a resampling consumer uses the scores as selection weights). All existing presets return boolean masks, so nothing breaks; the new ProportionalSelector(variables, column_mapping) preset returns normalize_proba(X[:, col]) (the deficit probability proportional to a column's value).
  • RandomSamplingTargetsGenerator takes a selector (breaking). The sampling_proba_func(y) kwarg is removed; the generator now resamples rows weighted by 1 - deficit_probability from a selector (noisy-OR combined over its variables), i.e. rows with a high deficit probability are dropped/under-sampled, rows with a low deficit probability are kept or replicated. Signature: generate(X, y=None, *, selector=None, replace=True, size=None); replace=True (default) may duplicate rows (importance resampling), replace=False gives a weighted thinning, size controls the output row count (default: input row count). The target y is no longer read for selection (columns of X instead). Migration: the old default (sample ∝ target values) becomes ProportionalSelector("col", {"col": idx}) over whichever X column holds the signal (e.g. the stacked target column), reading X rather than y.
  • RandomShiftClassesGenerator takes a selector (breaking). The class variable is read from a column of X (resolved via the selector's column_mapping), not from y; y is passed through unchanged. Signature: generate(X, y=None, *, selector=None, shift_std=0.1). The selector is REQUIRED (selector=None raises) — a per-class drift has no class-free default; fire masks are OR-ed. shift_std is now a float (one independent draw magnitude per class value) or a dict {class_value: std}; entries are SIGNED (|std| = draw scale, sign = direction). The per-dimension 2D-array form is removed (per-class shifts are isotropic — scale the data first for anisotropic drift). Class values absent from a dict are skipped. Migration: generate(X, y, shift_std=np.array([2., 2., 2., 2.])) → generate(np.column_stack([X, y]), y, selector=ClassSelector("cls", {"cls": n_features}, {"cls": {c: 1.0 for c in classes}}, rng=rng), shift_std=2.0).
  • Drift generators: signed per-column shift_std and class-column protection (breaking, RandomShiftGenerator/ RandomShiftClassesGenerator). shift_std entries are now signed: the magnitude (|shift_std|) is the scale of the normal draw and the sign is the shift direction — a negative entry drifts the column downward. For RandomShiftClassesGenerator the class column is identification metadata and is NEVER shifted by default (shifting it would move rows away from their class values); new parameters variables (columns to shift) and class_column (explicit class column position/name) allow shifting an explicit subset and/or a different class column. A dict shift_std={class_value: std} now requires a resolvable class column (raises otherwise).
  • Deterministic drift generators (new): FixedShiftGenerator and FixedShiftClassesGenerator — the non-random counterparts of the random shift generators. Each column is translated by exactly shift_std (in standard-deviation units, data standardized first; sign = direction); no random number is drawn, so repeated calls with the same input return the same output. Both are exported from badgers.generators.tabular_data.drift.
  • GaussianNoiseClassesGenerator takes a selector (breaking). Same contract as above: classes are a column of X resolved via the selector's column_mapping (selector=None raises; a per-class lookup requires selector.column_mapping to resolve the class column). y is now passed through UNCHANGED — the old implementation rebuilt yt as the class labels, silently discarding the original target (bug fixed). Signature: generate(X, y=None, *, selector=None, noise_std_per_class=dict()); fired rows whose class value is absent from the dict receive no noise.
  • do() and ScaledEdgeDGP are removed from the public API. They are replaced by the intervention/edition surface on the DGP protocol itself (see Added): a single data-level DGP.intervene and the structure edits as free functions in the new badgers.core.dgp.edits module (see below). ordered_descendants moved to badgers.core.causal_graph (still re-exported from badgers.core.dgp). Consequence for the causal defect generators: descendants of an intervention are recomputed with fresh noise (Pearl surgery) instead of propagating the delta with each node's exogenous noise preserved — the produced deficits are slightly "wider" (noise re-rolled downstream).
  • DGP structure-edit methods removed (breaking): scale_edge/remove_edge/exogenize/set_form (and the add_edge/reverse_edge stubs) are no longer methods on the DGP. The DGP is an immutable, fitted model with ONLY evaluation verbs (fit/response/draw_noise/sample/intervene); all structure modifications live as FREE FUNCTIONS in the new badgers.core.dgp.edits module (from badgers.core.dgp import edits): edits.scale_edge(dgp, child, parent, k), edits.remove_edge(dgp, child, parent), edits.add_edge_contribution(dgp, child, parent, contribution=... or coefficient=..., draw_noise=...) (the A5 cheap edit, ANM-scoped; cycle and existing-edge checks), edits.exogenize(dgp, node) (INTERVENTION-ONLY semantics — see below), edits.set_form(dgp, node, response_fn, draw_noise=None) (Q2: an optional noise-law closure). Edits return read-only views and never mutate the base DGP; they compose by delegation.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• New DGP backend GcmSCMDGP (dowhy extra): plug an externally built dowhy.gcm.StructuralCausalModel into badgers — mechanism fitting is delegated to gcm.fit, sampling and interventions run on the generic protocol with caller-provided rngs. Supports AdditiveNoiseModel (non-root), EmpiricalDistribution (root) and ClassifierFCM (non-root discrete nodes with numeric-encoded classes).
  • New DGP backend PyMCSCMDGP (pymc extra): plug a user-built PyMC causal model into badgers — structural nodes are observed RVs whose distribution parameters carry the structural functions; mechanism fitting is one joint pm.sample (full posterior kept), sampling and interventions run on the generic protocol with caller-provided rngs and ONE coherent posterior draw per cascade. Supported families: Normal, StudentT, Laplace (additive) and Bernoulli, Poisson, Binomial, Categorical (numeric-encoded discrete).

  • ClassSelector preset (badgers.core.selectors): per-class fixed-count sampling on a discrete column — ClassSelector(variables, column_mapping, proportions, rng=...) with proportions mapping each class column to {class_value: proportion}. Discovers the distinct values from the data (no manual class enumeration), raises ValueError on class values absent from the column (typo protection), and fires exactly min(int(prop * n_rows), n_rows_in_class) rows per listed class (partial mappings are legitimate: unlisted classes are kept). Class columns are columns of X resolved via column_mapping (selection does not read y -- the target is being deprecated as a data carrier). First subsampling consumer: RandomSamplingClassesGenerator.

  • Per-node DGP protocol (badgers.core.dgp package): DGP protocol and DGPMixin (topological fit/sample walk) — backends implement exactly one operation, fit_node(node, parents, data), and expose response(node, parent_values) and draw_noise(node, rng, n); sample(rng, n) is tier 2 and no generator depends on it.

  • pick_parameters hook (DGPMixin): called once at the top of the generic sample/intervene cascades; returns the DGP instance whose mechanisms drive the batch (ONE coherent parameter set per call). Default: self (deterministic backends fit exactly one parameter set). PyMCSCMDGP overrides it to pin ONE coherent posterior draw from the caller's rng (a _ParameterDrawView): each cascade evaluates one coherent parameterization; the carrier itself evaluates draw 0. Posterior draws compose through the structure edits (an edited view rebinds the pinned base). The generator API is unchanged — backends are swappable transparently.
  • Value-level intervention DGP.intervene(rows, nodes, values=None, *, rng=None) (Pearl surgery on given rows): fix the nodes at values (or at their current column values when values=None), recompute ALL their descendants in topological order with FRESH noise; upstream and non-descendant columns are untouched; intervened nodes stay pinned (an intervened descendant is not recomputed over its pinned value).
  • Structure edits as methods on the DGP (read-only views; the base DGP is never mutated; edits compose by delegation): scale_edge(child, parent, k) (edge reweighting without coefficient access; calibrate(data) evaluates the variance budget and raises ValueError when infeasible), remove_edge(child, parent) (= scale_edge(..., 0.0) — SCM-surgery view), exogenize(node) (make the node a root: incoming edges removed from the view's graph), set_form(node, response_fn) (replace one node's functional form with a user closure; noise law inherited — pending Q2). add_edge/reverse_edge raise NotImplementedError pending the training-data-retention decision (A3).
  • exogenize is INTERVENTION-ONLY (documented contract): designed for the pin-then-intervene flow (the generator writes the node's column; the cascade never recomputes a root). sample() on an exogenized DGP draws the node as 0 + N(0, residual_std) — NOT the real marginal; the empirical-resampling fix is deferred (it would require training-data retention).
  • CausalOutlierPropagationGenerator now propagates through the shared DGP machinery (internal change): the hand-rolled per-call lstsq forward pass is replaced by a fitted DGP (GcmSCMDGP from a dowhy-gcm SCM) + dgp.intervene(outliers, perturbation_nodes, rng=...) — uniform Pearl surgery semantics with the other causal generators. Behavior note: a degenerate zero-residual fitted mechanism now contributes no noise (the old 0.1*col_std fallback is gone).
  • Causal defect family (four generators sharing CausalGenerator, an explicit fit(X, graph, column_mapping) phase followed by generate(...) with selector= row gating): CausalDriftGenerator (single systematic shift, recomputed downstream), CausalNoiseGenerator (per-edge noise injection, noise_std), CausalImbalanceGenerator (quantile-range truncation (pure subset, descendants untouched) or explicit selector= — fired rows dropped), CausalMissingnessGenerator (m-graph missingness with any/all propagation, optional observation-graph derivation).

  • pymc optional extra (renamed from causal; pip install "badgers[pymc]") — only needed for building the PyMC SCM passed to PyMCSCMDGP.

  • TopQuantileSelector preset (badgers.core.selectors): fires rows at or above the quantile of a column — self mode (own column) or driver mode (a driver column, optionally broadcast to all gated variables). Deterministic (no rng); thresholds computed on the called rows or on a separate stats row set (for generators gating expanded rows against the original columns' statistics). All intensity parameters are now CONSTRUCTOR arguments of the presets (rate= for BernoulliSelector/ExactCountSelector, quantile= for TopQuantileSelector); __call__(X, y) takes no intensity kwarg, so an intensity sweep means constructing a new selector. The quantile is the direct quantile of the column (quantile=0.75 = everything at or above Q3). AlwaysSelector was added (the all-rows preset, the selector=None default of the causal generators).

  • CausalImbalanceGenerator now accepts an explicit selector= (additive; the old quantile_range rule remains the selector=None default): the rows FIRED by the selector are dropped (subsampling polarity, union over the selector's variables); perturbation_nodes/quantile_range are ignored when a selector is given, and perturbation_nodes is no longer required in selector mode.

  • DecompositionAndOutlierGenerator renamed to StructuredOutlierGenerator (old name kept as a backwards-compatible alias), with a new optional preprocessor= constructor argument: any sklearn pipeline-like object with transform/inverse_transform can replace the built-in standardization + decomposition — preprocessing is no longer hardcoded inside the generator.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text:
• Seaborn is no longer a dependency of the dev extra. All tutorial/dev notebooks use plain matplotlib for visualizations.
  • OlsDGP, DowhyGcmDGP and PyMCDGP DGP backends are removed. The only DGP backends are now the two SCM adapters (badgers.core.dgp.backends.GcmSCMDGP and PyMCSCMDGP): build the structural causal model with the wrapped library (dowhy-gcm or PyMC), then wrap it — GcmSCMDGP(scm) / PyMCSCMDGP(pymc_model). See docs/dev/Using-DGPs.ipynb.
  • edits.rebuild and edits.reversed_graph are removed (and with them CausalGenerator.rebuild_with_graph). Re-estimation after a structural modification is out of scope: build the modified SCM with the wrapped library's own API, fit it, and wrap it again with the appropriate adapter.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Causal generators require an explicit DGP (hard error when missing). There is no implicit default backend: every causal defect generator raises when no dgp= is supplied to the CausalGenerator constructor. Build a DGP from the library of choice (dowhy-gcm or PyMC) and wrap it with GcmSCMDGP/PyMCSCMDGP.
  • Drift tutorials and dev notebooks: extensive fixes — collapsed summary tables rebuilt, garbled prose fixed, one seeded rng per notebook (gen = Generator() naming, seed = 0, no global np.random), verification cells asserting the documented behavior (noise variance, constant drift shift, edge correlation/std preservation, class counts, NaN counts, repeat/drop lengths), and causal-outlier plots using get_outliers_labels().

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• New "Understanding badgers" concepts notebook (tutorials/concepts/Badgers-Concepts.ipynb): a step-by-step introduction — module structure, generator instantiation with an rng, generate(), shape rules (appending / gating / subsampling), the in-place mutation contract ("pass X.copy()"), the y deprecation, selectors, DGP backends and pipelines.
  • Tabular tutorials merged per deficit (one notebook per deficit instead of causal/non-causal pairs): Outliers.ipynb, Noise.ipynb, Missingness.ipynb, Imbalance.ipynb, Drift.ipynb. Each has Part A (acting on the observation process — no DGP) and Part B (acting on the DGP). Visualizations use explicit cls class vectors and labels deficit vectors (no y/yt placeholders); the outlier tutorial was substantially shortened (the causal part no longer repeats the concepts notebook).

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• CausalOutlierPropagationGenerator: New tabular generator that propagates outliers along causal-graph edges. First generator to rely on the causal-graph API.
  • Causal-graph utilities: validate_dag, topological_order, and related helpers for working with causal graphs.
  • Complete tabular generator benchmark coverage: All 16 tabular generators are now registered in the benchmark framework (up from 7). Added registrations for HistogramSamplingGenerator, ZScoreSamplingGenerator, LowDensitySamplingGenerator, HypersphereSamplingGenerator, GaussianNoiseClassesGenerator, RandomShiftClassesGenerator, RandomSamplingClassesGenerator, and RandomSamplingTargetsGenerator.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Generators now output NumPy arrays (breaking): Tabular and time-series generators return NumPy arrays instead of pandas DataFrames/Series. Input handling still accepts pandas DataFrames/Series.
  • Vectorized generators: Replaced per-row/per-column .iloc loops with batched NumPy operations for improved performance.
  • Two-tier sampler API: The sampler parameter is split into within_distribution_sampler and out_of_distribution_sampler.
  • Explicit column_mapping parameter: The causal-graph API now requires an explicit column_mapping parameter.
  • Benchmark outputs moved to .benchmarks/: Results and baselines are now stored in .benchmarks/results/ and .benchmarks/baselines/ (gitignored) instead of benchmarks/results/ and benchmarks/baselines/.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text: • node_to_index parameter from the causal-graph API (replaced by column_mapping).

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • Separated tests from benchmarks: Generator correctness tests now live in tests/generators/ as standalone pytest functions with fixtures, independent of the benchmark framework. The benchmarks/checks/ directory and FunctionalCheck infrastructure have been removed. Benchmarks now focus exclusively on performance measurement (time/memory). (9 commits: 943e230..56fee5d)

  • Test conftest files in tests/generators/{tabular_data,time_series,graph,text}/

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Install badgers with pip:

pip install badgers

Import badgers as any other library and start using it:

from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
from scipy.stats import norm
from badgers.generators.tabular_data.noise import AdditiveNoiseGenerator

X, y = make_blobs()
gen = AdditiveNoiseGenerator()
Xt, yt = gen.generate(X, y, distribution=norm(scale=0.5))

More examples are available in the tutorials section.

docs.title: Learn the concepts
docs.text: New to badgers? The Understanding badgers notebook explains the underlying objects and contracts step by step: library structure, how to instanciate generators, the generate() API, selectors, data-generating processes (DGP), pipelines and more.

docs.title: Build your own
docs.text:
Those interested in developing their own generators and/or contribute to badgers can have a look at the dev-tutorials section — three notebooks:

  • Creating Tabular Generators
  • Creating Selectors
  • Using DGPs — the shipped backends incl. the dowhy-gcm and PyMC SCM adapters on fit / sample / intervene

For the big picture, see the architecture overview and CONTRIBUTING.md.

The API documentation is also available in the API section.

def ordered_descendants(graph: nx.DiGraph, nodes) -> list:
    """Return the descendants of ``nodes``, in topological order.

    The nodes themselves are excluded (``nx.descendants`` semantics).

    Parameters
    ----------
    graph : nx.DiGraph
        A directed acyclic graph.
    nodes : one node or an iterable of nodes

    Returns
    -------
    list
        Descendants of ``nodes``, in topological order.
    """
    if isinstance(nodes, (str, bytes)):
        nodes = [nodes]
    else:
        try:
            nodes = list(nodes)
        except TypeError:
            nodes = [nodes]
    descendants = set()
    for node in nodes:
        descendants |= nx.descendants(graph, node)
    order = topological_order(graph)
    return [node for node in order if node in descendants]

def validate_dag(graph: nx.DiGraph) -> None:
    """
    Validate that the input is a directed acyclic graph.

    Parameters
    ----------
    graph : nx.DiGraph
        The graph to validate.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If graph is not a nx.DiGraph or contains cycles.
    """
    if not isinstance(graph, nx.DiGraph):
        raise ValueError(
            f"graph must be a nx.DiGraph, got {type(graph).__name__}"
        )
    if not nx.is_directed_acyclic_graph(graph):
        raise ValueError("graph is not a directed acyclic graph (contains cycles)")

class Pipeline:
    """
    Class for chaining different generators together.

    Not compatible with scikit-learn Pipelines
    """

    def __init__(self, generators: Dict):
        """
        Creates a Pipeline consisting of different generators
        :param generators: a dictionary containing as keys the generator names and as values the generators instances
        """
        self.generators = generators

    def generate(self, X, y, params: Dict = None):
        """
        Calls all generators generate function in the order

        :param X: the input features
        :param y: the class labels, regression targets, or None
        :param params: a dictionary containing as key: the generator names and
        as values: the parameters for each corresponding generate function
        :return: Xt, yt
        """
        if params is None:
            params = dict()
        for name, generator in self.generators.items():
            X, y = generator.generate(X, y, **params.get(name, dict()))
        return X, y

docs.title: sampling
docs.text:
Sampling strategies for generating values within or outside observed distributions.

WithinDistributionSampler subclasses generate plausible values from the observed data distribution (used for exogenous nodes in causal generation).

OutOfDistributionSampler subclasses generate anomalous values outside the observed distribution (used for perturbation nodes in causal generation).

Sample points on a hypersphere with radius >= 3 sigma.

Points are generated on a hypersphere with radius 3 + exponential(scale) in standardized space, then transformed back to the original scale.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
scale : float, default=1.0 Scale parameter for the exponential distribution.

Source code in badgers/core/sampling.py 
class HypersphereSampler(OutOfDistributionSampler):
    """Sample points on a hypersphere with radius >= 3 sigma.

    Points are generated on a hypersphere with radius
    ``3 + exponential(scale)`` in standardized space, then transformed
    back to the original scale.

    Parameters
    ----------
    scale : float, default=1.0
        Scale parameter for the exponential distribution.
    """

    def __init__(self, scale=1.0):
        self.scale = scale

    def sample(self, rng, X, columns, n_samples):
        n_features = len(columns)
        means = X[:, columns].mean(axis=0)
        stds = X[:, columns].std(axis=0)
        stds[stds == 0] = 1.0
        radii = 3.0 + rng.exponential(scale=self.scale, size=n_samples)
        standardized = random_spherical_coordinates(
            random_generator=rng,
            size=n_features,
            radii=radii,
        )
        return means + standardized * stds

class NormalSampler(WithinDistributionSampler):
    """Sample from N(mean, std) for each column independently."""

    def sample(self, rng, X, columns, n_samples):
        means = X[:, columns].mean(axis=0)
        stds = X[:, columns].std(axis=0)
        stds[stds == 0] = 1.0
        return rng.normal(loc=means, scale=stds, size=(n_samples, len(columns)))

docs.text:
Bases: OutOfDistributionSampler

Sample uniformly beyond the observed range.

Samples from [min - expansionrange, max + expansionrange] for each column independently.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
expansion : float Fraction to expand beyond [min, max]. Must be > 0.

Source code in badgers/core/sampling.py 
class UniformOutOfDistributionSampler(OutOfDistributionSampler):
    """Sample uniformly beyond the observed range.

    Samples from [min - expansion*range, max + expansion*range] for each
    column independently.

    Parameters
    ----------
    expansion : float
        Fraction to expand beyond [min, max]. Must be > 0.
    """

    def __init__(self, expansion):
        if expansion <= 0:
            raise ValueError(
                f"expansion must be > 0 for out-of-distribution sampling, "
                f"got {expansion}"
            )
        self.expansion = expansion

    def sample(self, rng, X, columns, n_samples):
        mins = X[:, columns].min(axis=0)
        maxs = X[:, columns].max(axis=0)
        ranges = maxs - mins
        low = mins - self.expansion * ranges
        high = maxs + self.expansion * ranges
        return rng.uniform(low=low, high=high, size=(n_samples, len(columns)))

class UniformSampler(WithinDistributionSampler):
    """Sample uniformly within [min, max] for each column.

    This sampler stays strictly within the observed range — no expansion.
    For out-of-distribution uniform sampling with expansion, use

        maxs = X[:, columns].max(axis=0)

docs.title: ZScoreSampler
docs.text:
Bases: OutOfDistributionSampler

Sample using z-score strategy: ±(3 + exponential) * sigma per column.

Each column independently gets a random sign, then a value of 3 + exponential(scale) standard deviations away from the mean.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
scale : float, default=1.0 Scale parameter for the exponential distribution.

Source code in badgers/core/sampling.py 
class ZScoreSampler(OutOfDistributionSampler):
    """Sample using z-score strategy: ±(3 + exponential) * sigma per column.

    Each column independently gets a random sign, then a value of
    ``3 + exponential(scale)`` standard deviations away from the mean.

    Parameters
    ----------
    scale : float, default=1.0
        Scale parameter for the exponential distribution.
    """

    def __init__(self, scale=1.0):
        self.scale = scale

    def sample(self, rng, X, columns, n_samples):
        n_features = len(columns)
        means = X[:, columns].mean(axis=0)
        stds = X[:, columns].std(axis=0)
        stds[stds == 0] = 1.0
        signs = random_sign(rng, size=(n_samples, n_features))
        exponentials = rng.exponential(
            scale=self.scale, size=(n_samples, n_features)
        )
        standardized = signs * (3.0 + exponentials)
        return means + standardized * stds

docs.title: selectors
docs.text:
Selectors: the observation-side contract for selecting deficit rows.

A SELECTOR decides which rows of the input get a data quality deficit

Selector = Callable[[X, y], dict[str, bool-mask | score]]
  • keys = variable names (the subscript in R_X: which column the mask gates)
  • values = per-row boolean masks or float SCORES, len(mask) == X.shape[0]
  • polarity: True/1.0 = R_X = 1 = deficit applied; False/0.0 = record as-is

Boolean masks are the common case, but a selector may return FLOAT scores in [0, 1]: the PROBABILITY that the deficit is applied to that row (the deterministic 1.0/0.0/bool values being the degenerate cases). A selector itself never draws randomness for these rates -- realization belongs to the consuming generator, which binds a single rng stream: a GATING consumer (noise, missingness) realizes p = 0.3 as a Bernoulli firing; a RESAMPLING consumer (imbalance) uses it as a selection weight. Being in core, the module is modality-agnostic: time-series / graph / text generators can reuse the same contract with masks over their own axes.

The presets are small callable objects so their configuration (which variables, which rng, which column mapping, which intensity) stays introspectable (repr and stored attributes). The FIRE INTENSITY is part of the preset configuration where it exists: rate for the stochastic presets (BernoulliSelector/ExactCountSelector), quantile for the deterministic TopQuantileSelector, and proportions for the per-class ClassSelector are constructor arguments, so an intensity sweep means constructing a new selector (nothing is swept on the call). The trivial AlwaysSelector has no intensity knob at all. There is deliberately no base class and no registry -- conformance to the :class:Selector protocol is defined by the call signature alone. Each preset is self-contained: its mask logic is inlined in __call__ (no free helper functions), so a preset depends on nothing beyond numpy and the consuming generators simply construct one and call it.

GATING consumers preserve the input's shape and only ALTER the fired cells (missingness, noise, outliers, ...); SUBSAMPLING consumers (imbalance) DROP the fired rows, so their output is smaller than the input. The contract itself is only "which rows fire".

The trivial, value- and rng-free rule — the degenerate gate "apply the deficit everywhere". The default when a causal generator receives selector=None (noise, drift, edge perturbation).

class AlwaysSelector:
    """Selector: every row fires, for every gated variable.

    The trivial, value- and rng-free rule — the degenerate gate "apply the
    deficit everywhere". The default when a causal generator receives
    ``selector=None`` (noise, drift, edge perturbation).

    Parameters
    ----------
    variables : str or sequence of str
        Names of the gated variables (the returned dict's keys).

    Calling
    -------
    ``__call__(X, y=None)``: returns an all-True mask per variable. No
    intensity kwarg — there is nothing to sweep (any intensity knob lives
    in the DEFICIT itself, e.g. noise_std).
    """

    def __init__(self, variables: str | Sequence[str]):
        self.variables = _validate_variables(variables)

    def __call__(
        self,
        X: np.ndarray,
        y: np.ndarray | None = None,
    ) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
        return {
            name: np.ones(X.shape[0], dtype=bool)
            for name in self.variables
        }

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return f"AlwaysSelector(variables={self.variables!r})"

Selector: iid per-row, per-variable deficit indicator draws.

For each requested variable, whether a row is affected (R = 1) is an independent Bernoulli draw with probability rate, independent of the data values and of y. In the missingness literature this pattern is called "completely at random"; the class name here describes the RULE (iid Bernoulli firing), not the deficit, because the same rule gates any observation-side deficit form (missing values, noise, out-of-distribution values, ...).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: variables : str or sequence of str Name(s) of the variables this selector gates: one dict key and one INDEPENDENT mask per name (a single vectorized 2D draw). Names are graph-node names -- X/y are positional numpy arrays, so the consuming generator resolves names to column positions via its column_mapping (the same binding as for rng). This selector never reads column values (value-free rule). rng : numpy.random.Generator or None, default=None Random generator used for the draws. The consuming generator binds its own generator here (single RNG stream). Calling without a bound generator raises ValueError.

docs.title: Calling
docs.text: __call__(X, y=None): returns one mask per variable.

docs.title: Examples

import numpy as np selector = BernoulliSelector("temperature", rate=0.3, ... rng=np.random.default_rng(0)) X = np.arange(20.0).reshape(10, 2) masks = selector(X, y=None) list(masks) == ["temperature"] True masks["temperature"].dtype dtype('bool')

A list of variables yields one independent mask per variable:

selector = BernoulliSelector(["a", "b"], rate=0.5, ... rng=np.random.default_rng(0)) sorted(selector(X, y=None)) ['a', 'b']

class BernoulliSelector:
    """Selector: iid per-row, per-variable deficit indicator draws.

    For each requested variable, whether a row is affected (``R = 1``) is an
    independent Bernoulli draw with probability ``rate``, independent of the
    data values and of ``y``. In the missingness literature this pattern is
    called "completely at random"; the class name here describes the RULE
    (iid Bernoulli firing), not the deficit, because the same rule gates any
    observation-side deficit form (missing values, noise, out-of-distribution
    values, ...).

    Parameters
    ----------
    variables : str or sequence of str
        Name(s) of the variables this selector gates: one dict key and one
        INDEPENDENT mask per name (a single vectorized 2D draw). Names are
        graph-node names -- ``X``/``y`` are positional numpy arrays, so the
        consuming generator resolves names to column positions via its
        column_mapping (the same binding as for ``rng``). This selector never
        reads column values (value-free rule).
    rng : numpy.random.Generator or None, default=None
        Random generator used for the draws. The consuming generator binds
        its own generator here (single RNG stream). Calling without a bound
        generator raises ``ValueError``.

    Calling
    -------
    ``__call__(X, y=None)``: returns one mask per variable.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> selector = BernoulliSelector("temperature", rate=0.3,
    ...                              rng=np.random.default_rng(0))
    >>> X = np.arange(20.0).reshape(10, 2)
    >>> masks = selector(X, y=None)
    >>> list(masks) == ["temperature"]
    True
    >>> masks["temperature"].dtype
    dtype('bool')

    A list of variables yields one independent mask per variable:

    >>> selector = BernoulliSelector(["a", "b"], rate=0.5,
    ...                              rng=np.random.default_rng(0))
    >>> sorted(selector(X, y=None))
    ['a', 'b']
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        variables: str | Sequence[str],
        rate: float,
        rng: np.random.Generator | None = None,
    ):
        self.variables = _validate_variables(variables)
        self.rate = _validate_rate(rate, "rate")
        self.rng = rng

    def __call__(
        self,
        X: np.ndarray,
        y: np.ndarray | None = None,
    ) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
        if self.rng is None:
            raise ValueError(
                f"{self!r} has no random generator bound: construct it with "
                "rng=numpy.random.Generator (the consuming generator binds "
                "its own) or set selector.rng before calling."
            )
        # One vectorized iid draw: shape (n_rows, k), True = deficit applied.
        draws = (
            self.rng.random(size=(X.shape[0], len(self.variables)))
            < self.rate
        )
        return {name: draws[:, i] for i, name in enumerate(self.variables)}

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return (
            f"BernoulliSelector(variables={self.variables!r}, "
            f"rate={self.rate!r})"
        )

docs.title: ClassSelector
docs.text:
Selector: fires a fixed share of the rows of each class of a column.

For each gated variable (a column of X intended to hold DISCRETE values -- classes), the distinct values are discovered from X and for every class value listed in proportions exactly min(int(prop * n_rows), n_rows_in_class) rows OF THAT CLASS are drawn WITHOUT REPLACEMENT (uniform) -- the proportion is a share of the TOTAL row count, clipped to the rows available in the class. Class values present in the column but absent from the mapping are NOT fired (kept as-is) -- partial mappings are legitimate ("only rarefy the rare class"). The FIRE INTENSITY (the proportions) is a constructor argument: a sweep means constructing a new selector.

Like the other presets, the class name describes the RULE (per-class fixed-count sampling), never the deficit that follows. The consuming generator decides what firing means -- e.g. the imbalance generators DROP the fired rows (subsampling deficit).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: variables : str or sequence of str Names of the class columns gated by this selector (the returned dict's keys). Each must be a key of column_mapping. column_mapping : dict mapping str -> int Maps each variable name to its column index in X (standard binding; this preset READS values). proportions : dict mapping str -> dict For each variable name, a mapping {class_value: proportion} with proportions in [0, 1]. Proportions are shares of the INPUT row count. A class value in the mapping that is absent from the column raises ValueError (typo protection). rng : numpy.random.Generator or None, default=None Random generator used for the draws. The consuming generator binds its own generator here (single RNG stream). Calling without a bound generator raises ValueError.

docs.title: Calling
docs.text: __call__(X, y=None): one mask per class column; a row fires if it belongs to a fired class. With several class columns the masks are INDEPENDENT per column -- consumers typically OR them (a row dropped if fired in any column). y is unused: class columns are columns of X (the target is being deprecated as a data carrier).

class ClassSelector:
    """Selector: fires a fixed share of the rows of each class of a column.

    For each gated variable (a column of ``X`` intended to hold DISCRETE
    values -- classes), the distinct values are discovered from ``X`` and
    for every class value listed in ``proportions`` exactly
    ``min(int(prop * n_rows), n_rows_in_class)`` rows OF THAT CLASS are
    drawn WITHOUT REPLACEMENT (uniform) -- the proportion is a share of
    the TOTAL row count, clipped to the rows available in the class.
    Class values present in the column but absent from the
    mapping are NOT fired (kept as-is) -- partial mappings are legitimate
    ("only rarefy the rare class"). The FIRE INTENSITY (the proportions)
    is a constructor argument: a sweep means constructing a new selector.

    Like the other presets, the class name describes the RULE (per-class
    fixed-count sampling), never the deficit that follows. The consuming
    generator decides what firing means -- e.g. the imbalance generators
    DROP the fired rows (subsampling deficit).

    Parameters
    ----------
    variables : str or sequence of str
        Names of the class columns gated by this selector (the returned
        dict's keys). Each must be a key of ``column_mapping``.
    column_mapping : dict mapping str -> int
        Maps each variable name to its column index in ``X`` (standard
        binding; this preset READS values).
    proportions : dict mapping str -> dict
        For each variable name, a mapping ``{class_value: proportion}``
        with proportions in ``[0, 1]``. Proportions are shares of the
        INPUT row count. A class value in the mapping that is absent from
        the column raises ``ValueError`` (typo protection).
    rng : numpy.random.Generator or None, default=None
        Random generator used for the draws. The consuming generator binds
        its own generator here (single RNG stream). Calling without a
        bound generator raises ``ValueError``.

    Calling
    -------
    ``__call__(X, y=None)``: one mask per class column; a row fires if it
    belongs to a fired class. With several class columns the masks are
    INDEPENDENT per column -- consumers typically OR them (a row dropped
    if fired in any column). ``y`` is unused: class columns are columns
    of ``X`` (the target is being deprecated as a data carrier).

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> X = np.array([0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1], dtype=float).reshape(-1, 1)
    >>> mapping = {"cls": 0}
    >>> selector = ClassSelector("cls", mapping, {"cls": {0: 2 / 3}},
    ...                          rng=np.random.default_rng(0))
    >>> mask = selector(X)["cls"]
    >>> int(mask.sum())
    2
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        variables: str | Sequence[str],
        column_mapping: dict[str, int],
        proportions: dict[str, dict],
        rng: np.random.Generator | None = None,
    ):
        self.variables = _validate_variables(variables)
        for name in self.variables:
            if name not in column_mapping:
                raise ValueError(
                    f"variable {name!r} not in column_mapping"
                )
            if name not in proportions:
                raise ValueError(
                    f"variable {name!r} has no entry in proportions"
                )
            for class_value, prop in proportions[name].items():
                _validate_rate(prop, f"proportions[{name!r}][{class_value!r}]")
        self.column_mapping = column_mapping
        self.proportions = proportions
        self.rng = rng

    def __call__(
        self,
        X: np.ndarray,
        y: np.ndarray | None = None,
    ) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
        if self.rng is None:
            raise ValueError(
                f"{self!r} has no random generator bound: construct it with "
                "rng=numpy.random.Generator (the consuming generator binds "
                "its own) or set selector.rng before calling."
            )
        n_rows = X.shape[0]
        masks = {}
        for name in self.variables:
            col = X[:, self.column_mapping[name]]
            values = set(np.unique(col).tolist())
            unknown = [v for v in self.proportions[name] if v not in values]
            if unknown:
                raise ValueError(
                    f"class value(s) {unknown!r} not found in column "
                    f"{name!r} (found {sorted(values)!r})"
                )
            mask = np.zeros(n_rows, dtype=bool)
            for class_value, prop in self.proportions[name].items():
                rows = np.flatnonzero(col == class_value)
                # Shares are of the TOTAL row count; clipped to the number
                # of rows actually in the class (a mask cannot fire a row
                # twice, so no replacement is possible).
                count = min(int(prop * n_rows), len(rows))
                # Sampling without replacement: sequential by nature -- the
                # documented exception to the vectorization rule.
                idx = self.rng.choice(rows, size=count, replace=False)
                mask[idx] = True
            masks[name] = mask
        return masks

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return (
            f"ClassSelector(variables={self.variables!r}, "
            f"proportions={self.proportions!r})"
        )

docs.title: ExactCountSelector
docs.text:
Selector: exactly int(rate * n_rows) rows per variable, drawn without replacement (uniform, or weighted by per-row probabilities).

The exact-count sibling of :class:BernoulliSelector (random count). This is the rule behind the classic missingness generators: per variable, a fixed number of affected rows, optionally with per-row selection probabilities ("soft" coupling -- the probability of being affected varies smoothly with the data instead of a hard quantile threshold).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: variables : str or sequence of str Variable names gated by this selector; one INDEPENDENT mask per name (rows are drawn separately per variable). weights : None, (n_rows, len(variables)) array, or callable Per-row selection probabilities. None = uniform. An array must have shape (X.shape[0], len(variables)) with non-negative entries summing to (approximately) 1 per column -- pass them through :func:badgers.core.utils.normalize_proba first if needed. A callable (X, y=None) -> (n_rows, k) array is evaluated per call -- this is how data-driven coupling is expressed (the caller binds any randomness, e.g. rng, inside the callable). rng : numpy.random.Generator or None, default=None Random generator used for the draws. The consuming generator binds its own generator here (single RNG stream). Calling without a bound generator raises ValueError.

docs.title: Calling
docs.text: __call__(X, y=None): the affected count is int(rate * n_rows) (floor, classic semantics).

class ExactCountSelector:
    """Selector: exactly ``int(rate * n_rows)`` rows per variable, drawn
    without replacement (uniform, or weighted by per-row probabilities).

    The exact-count sibling of :class:`BernoulliSelector` (random count).
    This is the rule behind the classic missingness generators: per
    variable, a fixed number of affected rows, optionally with per-row
    selection probabilities ("soft" coupling -- the probability of being
    affected varies smoothly with the data instead of a hard quantile
    threshold).

    Parameters
    ----------
    variables : str or sequence of str
        Variable names gated by this selector; one INDEPENDENT mask per
        name (rows are drawn separately per variable).
    weights : None, (n_rows, len(variables)) array, or callable
        Per-row selection probabilities. ``None`` = uniform. An array
        must have shape ``(X.shape[0], len(variables))`` with non-negative
        entries summing to (approximately) 1 per column -- pass them
        through :func:`badgers.core.utils.normalize_proba` first if
        needed. A callable ``(X, y=None) -> (n_rows, k)`` array is
        evaluated per call -- this is how data-driven coupling is
        expressed (the caller binds any randomness, e.g. rng, inside the
        callable).
    rng : numpy.random.Generator or None, default=None
        Random generator used for the draws. The consuming generator
        binds its own generator here (single RNG stream). Calling without
        a bound generator raises ``ValueError``.

    Calling
    -------
    ``__call__(X, y=None)``: the affected count is ``int(rate * n_rows)``
    (floor, classic semantics).

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> selector = ExactCountSelector("temperature", rate=0.4,
    ...                               rng=np.random.default_rng(0))
    >>> X = np.arange(20.0).reshape(10, 2)
    >>> selector(X, y=None)["temperature"].sum()
    4
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        variables: str | Sequence[str],
        rate: float,
        weights: np.ndarray
        | Callable[[np.ndarray, np.ndarray | None], np.ndarray]
        | None = None,
        rng: np.random.Generator | None = None,
    ):
        self.variables = _validate_variables(variables)
        self.rate = _validate_rate(rate, "rate")
        self.weights = weights
        self.rng = rng

    def _resolve_weights(
        self, X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray | None
    ) -> np.ndarray | None:
        k = len(self.variables)
        if self.weights is None:
            return None
        w = self.weights(X, y) if callable(self.weights) else self.weights
        w = np.asarray(w, dtype=float)
        if w.shape != (X.shape[0], k):
            raise ValueError(
                f"weights must have shape ({X.shape[0]}, {k}), got {w.shape}"
            )
        if (w < 0).any():
            raise ValueError("weights must be non-negative")
        return w

    def __call__(
        self,
        X: np.ndarray,
        y: np.ndarray | None = None,
    ) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
        if self.rng is None:
            raise ValueError(
                f"{self!r} has no random generator bound: construct it with "
                "rng=numpy.random.Generator (the consuming generator binds "
                "its own) or set selector.rng before calling."
            )
        n_rows = X.shape[0]
        count = int(self.rate * n_rows)
        # Resolve the weights BEFORE the row draws: data-driven coupling
        # may consume rng draws itself (e.g. choosing driver columns), and
        # those must precede the per-variable row draws (draw-order parity
        # with the classic generators).
        weights = self._resolve_weights(X, y)
        masks = {}
        for i, name in enumerate(self.variables):
            # Sampling without replacement: sequential by nature -- the
            # documented exception to the vectorization rule.
            p = None if weights is None else weights[:, i]
            idx = self.rng.choice(n_rows, size=count, replace=False, p=p)
            mask = np.zeros(n_rows, dtype=bool)
            mask[idx] = True
            masks[name] = mask
        return masks

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return (
            f"ExactCountSelector(variables={self.variables!r}, "
            f"rate={self.rate!r}, "
            f"weights={'callable' if callable(self.weights) else self.weights!r})"
        )

docs.title: ProportionalSelector
docs.text:
Selector: the deficit probability is proportional to a column's value.

Value-driven, FRACTIONAL rule: for each gated variable the per-row deficit probability is derived from the column's values, rescaled to [0, 1] (min-max) and then normalized to sum to 1. A constant column yields the uniform probability. Deterministic (no rng); the consumer decides how the probabilities are realized (weights in a weighted draw, Bernoulli firing, ...). "Proportional" describes the RULE, never the deficit that follows.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: variables : str or sequence of str Names of the gated variables (the returned dict's keys). Each must be a key of column_mapping. column_mapping : dict mapping str -> int Maps each variable name to its column index in X (standard binding; this preset READS values).

docs.title: Calling
docs.text: __call__(X, y=None): one float score array per variable (the normalized column values, summing to 1).

class ProportionalSelector:
    """Selector: the deficit probability is proportional to a column's value.

    Value-driven, FRACTIONAL rule: for each gated variable the per-row
    deficit probability is derived from the column's values, rescaled to
    ``[0, 1]`` (min-max) and then normalized to sum to 1. A constant
    column yields the uniform probability. Deterministic (no ``rng``); the
    consumer decides how the probabilities are realized (weights in a
    weighted draw, Bernoulli firing, ...). "Proportional" describes the
    RULE, never the deficit that follows.

    Parameters
    ----------
    variables : str or sequence of str
        Names of the gated variables (the returned dict's keys). Each must
        be a key of ``column_mapping``.
    column_mapping : dict mapping str -> int
        Maps each variable name to its column index in ``X`` (standard
        binding; this preset READS values).

    Calling
    -------
    ``__call__(X, y=None)``: one float score array per variable (the
    normalized column values, summing to 1).

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> X = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 4.0]).reshape(-1, 1)
    >>> ProportionalSelector("f0", {"f0": 0})(X)["f0"]
    array([0.        , 0.33333333, 0.66666667])
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        variables: str | Sequence[str],
        column_mapping: dict[str, int],
    ):
        self.variables = _validate_variables(variables)
        for name in self.variables:
            if name not in column_mapping:
                raise ValueError(
                    f"variable {name!r} not in column_mapping"
                )
        self.column_mapping = column_mapping

    def __call__(
        self,
        X: np.ndarray,
        y: np.ndarray | None = None,
    ) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
        scores = {}
        for name in self.variables:
            col = X[:, self.column_mapping[name]].astype(float)
            span = col.max() - col.min()
            unit = (col - col.min()) / span if span > 0 else np.ones_like(col)
            scores[name] = normalize_proba(unit)
        return scores

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return (
            f"ProportionalSelector(variables={self.variables!r})"
        )

Bases: Protocol

Protocol for selectors: callables producing per-variable deficit masks.

Implementations (preset objects or user callables) must accept (X, y=None) and return a dict[str, numpy.ndarray] mapping each gated variable name to a boolean mask with one entry per input row, True meaning the deficit is applied to that row.

Note: isinstance checks against this (runtime-checkable) protocol only verify that the object is callable, not the full signature. All intensity configuration lives in the constructor. Return values may be boolean masks (deterministic fire) or float SCORES in [0, 1] (the probability that the deficit is applied); the consuming generator realizes fractional scores appropriately (Bernoulli firing for gating consumers, selection weights for resampling consumers).

docs.title: TopQuantileSelector
docs.text:
Selector: fires rows above the quantile of a column.

Deterministic, value-driven rule: for each gated variable the threshold is quantile(col, quantile) and a row fires when the compared value is >= threshold. E.g. quantile=0.75 fires every row whose value is at or above the third quartile (Q3) -- "I keep everything above Q3". Like the other presets, the class name describes the RULE (quantile thresholding), never the deficit that follows.

Two modes:

  • self (drivers=None): each variable fires rows where its OWN value is above its own quantile.
  • driver (drivers=...): each variable fires rows where a DRIVER column's value is above the driver's quantile. A single string is broadcast to all variables (one driver gates everything); a sequence gives one driver per variable (same length as variables).

Because the rule is deterministic, no rng is needed.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: variables : str or sequence of str Names of the gated variables (the returned dict's keys). column_mapping : dict mapping str -> int Maps each variable/driver name to its column index in X. Required because this preset READS values (unlike the other presets, which are value-blind). quantile : float, in [0, 1] The quantile of the (driver) column that forms the threshold. The comparison is >=, so with quantile=1.0 rows equal to the column maximum still fire. Baked at construction: a configured selector is self-contained. drivers : str, sequence of str, or None, default=None The driver columns as described above.

docs.title: Calling
docs.text:
__call__(X, y=None): one mask per gated variable; a row fires when the (driver) column's value is >= the column's quantile threshold computed on the passed rows.
